evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ortuño et al., 2014 and Reinagel et al., 1999.

claim: Bursts were rarely triggered by optogenetic activation, with burst percentage of total spikes amounting to 0.7 ± 0.3% for the example neuron.
source: For the example neuron (Figure 2A), bursts were rarely triggered and burst percentage of total spikes amounted to 0.7 ± 0.3%, with other recorded neurons also in this range (n = 7, range: 0.03–3.0%).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of burst activity in recorded neurons.

claim: Optogenetic LGN activation elicited mostly tonic spikes, consistent with reports of a moderate propensity for bursting in tree shrew LGN.
source: Optogenetic LGN activation thus elicited mostly tonic spikes, consistent with reports of a moderate propensity for bursting in tree shrew LGN (Wei et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis and a citation to Wei et al., 2011.

claim: 12 LGN neurons in two animals were significantly phase-locked at least at one of the flicker frequencies.
source: We found 12 LGN neurons in two animals that were significantly phase-locked (Rayleigh test p<0.05) at least at one of the flicker frequencies and across this population the magnitude of phase locking did not differ significantly over the four frequencies tested (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by phase-locking analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The magnitude of phase locking did not differ significantly over the four frequencies tested.
source: We found 12 LGN neurons in two animals that were significantly phase-locked (Rayleigh test p<0.05) at least at one of the flicker frequencies and across this population the magnitude of phase locking did not differ significantly over the four frequencies tested (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of phase-locking data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Tree shrew LGN layers are specialized for ON- and OFF-type visual inputs.
source: Tree shrew LGN layers are specialized for ON- and OFF-type visual inputs (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Conway and Schiller, 1983), responding to onset of bright and dark targets with respect to background illumination, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Conway and Schiller, 1983 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Local recordings of LGN neural activity at the site of light stimulation can be used to functionally identify the stimulated layer.
source: Local recordings of LGN neural activity at the site of light stimulation can thus be used to functionally identify the stimulated layer, as illustrated for 1 Hz and 5 Hz full-field bright visual stimulation (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: These results suggest robust expression of ChR2 in thalamocortical relay cells across tree shrew LGN layers under the CamKIIα promotor.
source: Together, these results suggest robust expression of ChR2 in thalamocortical relay cells across tree shrew LGN layers under the CamKIIα promotor.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the functional validation experiments.

claim: Tree shrews were trained on a visual detection task where they had to enter a nose poke and respond to the onset of a visual stimulus by withdrawing from the nose poke.
source: To examine whether animals could detect LGN optogenetic activation, we first trained them on a visual detection task, where they had to enter a nose poke on a transparent horizontal platform at the center of a 70-cm-diameter opaque sphere and respond to the onset of a visual stimulus by withdrawing from the nose poke (see 'Materials and methods,' Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is stated as a description of the experimental methods and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A 2° visual stimulus composed of a cloud of moving white dots was used to facilitate the subsequent transition to the optogenetic stimulation detection task.
source: We used a 2° visual stimulus composed of a cloud of moving white dots to facilitate the subsequent transition to the optogenetic stimulation detection task.
evidence: The claim is stated as a description of the experimental design rationale.

claim: Artificial visual percepts correspond better to moving clouds of dots rather than oriented bars or grating stimuli.
source: Although artificial visual percepts can take on a variety of forms, they correspond better to moving clouds of dots rather than oriented bars or grating stimuli (Fernández et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fernández et al., 2021.

claim: The animals' response times are narrowly distributed and largely follow the target onset time with a median response time of 290 ms.
source: It is evident that the animals' response times are narrowly distributed and largely follow the target onset time marked by the thick oblique line with a median response time of 290 ms and an overall correct performance of 76%.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data analysis.

claim: Overall correct performance was 76% for the example tree shrew.
source: It is evident that the animals' response times are narrowly distributed and largely follow the target onset time marked by the thick oblique line with a median response time of 290 ms and an overall correct performance of 76%.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data analysis.

claim: All animals showed improved d' sensitivity over the course of learning, reaching d' values between 1 and 2.5 at the end of training.
source: Group data for the six tree shrews participating in this experiment is shown in Figure 3D, illustrating that all animals showed improved d' sensitivity over the course of learning, reaching d' values between 1 and 2.5 at the end of training.
evidence: The claim is supported by group data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The d' sensitivity over the last four training days was significantly different from zero in all animals.
source: The d' sensitivity over the last four training days was significantly different from zero in all animals (t-test, p<0.01), confirming that all animals had acquired the visual detection task.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: All animals readily generalized detection performance up to 120° eccentricity.
source: All animals readily generalized detection performance up to 120° (Figure 3E and F), with performance declining at 150°, the highest eccentricity tested, in all except one animal (959), which detected these peripheral moving dot stimuli without apparent problems.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Performance declined at 150° eccentricity in all except one animal (959).
source: All animals readily generalized detection performance up to 120° (Figure 3E and F), with performance declining at 150°, the highest eccentricity tested, in all except one animal (959), which detected these peripheral moving dot stimuli without apparent problems.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: All tree shrews generalized significantly from the center position to eccentric stimulus presentation.
source: Eccentricity effects were studied in only a single session per eccentricity value; however, all tree shrews generalized significantly from the center position to eccentric stimulus presentation (t-tests comparing d' at four studied eccentricities against zero, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Bias tended to increase with eccentricity as animals increasingly missed targets.
source: Bias tended to increase with eccentricity (Figure 3G) as animals increasingly missed targets.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Tree shrews can acquire the visual detection task and generalize across the visual field in a freely moving unrestrained behavioral setting, achieving d' values of up to 2.5 within a week of training.
source: Taken together, behavioral data on the visual detection task indicates that tree shrews can acquire this task and generalize across the visual field in a freely moving unrestrained behavioral setting, achieving d' values of up to 2.5 within a week of training.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: LGN-implanted animals achieved d' sensitivity values around ≥1.0.
source: We note that LGN-implanted animals achieved d' sensitivity values around ≥1.0, whereas d' did not surpass 0.5 in control animals implanted outside the LGN (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for a comparison of maximum d' values in visual and optogenetic detection tasks).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B and C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: d' did not surpass 0.5 in control animals implanted outside the LGN.
source: We note that LGN-implanted animals achieved d' sensitivity values around ≥1.0, whereas d' did not surpass 0.5 in control animals implanted outside the LGN (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for a comparison of maximum d' values in visual and optogenetic detection tasks).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B and C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tree shrews can readily detect optogenetic activation of the visual thalamocortical pathway.
source: This suggests that tree shrews can readily detect optogenetic activation of the visual thalamocortical pathway.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data comparing LGN-implanted and control animals.

claim: Higher amplitudes of stimulation tended to be detected most readily.
source: Generally, higher amplitudes of stimulation tended to be detected most readily, as would be expected.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data analysis.

claim: Two animals (1111, 1409) appeared to respond best to 10 Hz stimulation.
source: In terms of light stimulation frequency, two animals (1111, 1409) appeared to respond best to 10 Hz stimulation while for one animal (959) the preferred frequency was 50 Hz.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data analysis.

claim: For one animal (959) the preferred frequency was 50 Hz.
source: In terms of light stimulation frequency, two animals (1111, 1409) appeared to respond best to 10 Hz stimulation while for one animal (959) the preferred frequency was 50 Hz.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data analysis.

claim: Tree shrews showed evidence for rapid generalization from the visual to the optogenetic stimulation.
source: Importantly, tree shrews showed evidence for rapid generalization from the visual to the optogenetic stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tree shrews reliably detected optogenetic stimulation as evidenced by significant d' values.
source: The results, shown in Figure 5, highlight that tree shrews reliably detected optogenetic stimulation as evidenced by significant d' values (two-way ANOVA main effect, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A significant effect of bias between animals is apparent, suggestive of differences in strategy during the optogenetic detection task.
source: A significant effect of bias between animals is apparent (one-way ANOVA, p<0.05), suggestive of differences in strategy during the optogenetic detection task, with tree shrew 1409 showing significantly negative bias.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: These findings document the reproducibility of tree shrew behavioral detection of optogenetic LGN activation.
source: These findings document the reproducibility of tree shrew behavioral detection of optogenetic LGN activation.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: Significant activation was observed in 22 out of 111 LGN MUA sites.
source: We observed significant activation in 22 out of 111 LGN MUA sites, but only in 5 of 111 V1 MUA sites (paired t-tests: p<0.05, Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Significant activation was observed in only 5 of 111 V1 MUA sites.
source: We observed significant activation in 22 out of 111 LGN MUA sites, but only in 5 of 111 V1 MUA sites (paired t-tests: p<0.05, Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Many of the activated LGN sites showed a robust, short latency response motif to stimulation.
source: Many of the activated LGN sites showed a robust, short latency response motif to stimulation (see example unit in Figure 6A), while our recordings contained only relatively weakly modulated V1 MUA sites at short latency.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The MUA at some LGN and V1 sites exhibited offset responses following the termination of the light stimulation.
source: We observed that the MUA at some LGN and V1 sites exhibited offset responses following the termination of the light stimulation (LGN: n = 16, V1: n = 8, paired t-tests: p<0.05, Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Robust offset responses were evident in both LGN and V1 and had response latencies of around 50 ms following the cessation of stimulation in both areas.
source: Robust offset responses were evident in both LGN and V1 (see Figure 6B) and had response latencies of around 50 ms following the cessation of stimulation in both areas, consistent with a neural circuit origin of these effects involving recurrent processing and inhibitory modulations.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The unit data highlights that LGN optogenetic stimulation robustly drives local units.
source: The unit data highlights that LGN optogenetic stimulation robustly drives local units, and while it was more difficult to isolate V1 units directly modulated by optogenetic stimulation, possibly due to incomplete overlap of the stimulated thalamocortical recipient zone with the receptive field of the V1 MUA activity.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data.

claim: 29/111 V1 sites showed significant 40 Hz entrainment.
source: Indeed, 29/111 V1 sites showed significant 40 Hz entrainment (paired t-test: p<0.01), and traces from an example site illustrate high-amplitude 40 Hz oscillations during stimulation on two single trials as well as the average across repetitions (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Only 11/111 LGN sites showed significant modulations in LFPs.
source: The thalamic LFPs were by comparison rather insensitive to light stimulation, with only 11/111 sites showing significant modulations (paired t-test: p<0.01; χ2-test comparing LGN and V1; p<0.01, see Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Endogenously generated LFPs during the baseline period in LGN were much lower in magnitude than in V1.
source: Endogenously generated LFPs during the baseline period in LGN were much lower in magnitude than in V1 (for 40 Hz unpaired t-tests: p<<0.001) since unlike V1 the LGN does not possess systematically aligned dendritic structures that underlie LFP activations (Rainer, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of LFP data and a citation to Rainer, 2019.

claim: Laser-induced spikes in the LGN were reliably followed by depth negative potentials in V1 at a latency of ≈3 ms.
source: We found that laser-induced spikes in the LGN were reliably followed by depth negative potentials in V1 at a latency of ≈3 ms, which is similar to the latency of the V1 excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) triggered by monosynaptic input from LGN neurons reported in the cat (Sedigh-Sarvestani et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by spike-triggered average analysis and a citation to Sedigh-Sarvestani et al., 2017.

claim: Activation of CaMKIIα LGN neurons is capable of modulating V1 responses at the earliest stages of cortical processing.
source: As the LFP is thought to primarily reflect synchronized synaptic inputs, this indicates that activation of CaMKIIα LGN neurons is capable of modulating V1 responses at the earliest stages of cortical processing.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed latency of V1 LFP responses to LGN spiking.

claim: The V1 LFP was spectrally coherent with evoked LGN spiking across the gamma frequency range (30–80 Hz).
source: Additionally, the V1 LFP was spectrally coherent with evoked LGN spiking across the gamma frequency range (30–80 Hz).
evidence: The claim is supported by spike field coherence analysis.

claim: Out of a population of 22 V1 sites that showed significant increases in 40 Hz power following optogenetic activation, 9 of these sites also exhibited significant coherence with LGN spiking at 40 Hz.
source: Indeed, out of a population of 22 V1 sites that showed significant increases in 40 Hz power following optogenetic activation, 9 of these sites also exhibited significant coherence with LGN spiking at 40 Hz (see Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by spike field coherence analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The time of first negative peak of the STA was taken as the response latency to the thalamic spikes, M = 3.8 ± 1.5 ms (n = 9).
source: We took the time of first negative peak of the STA as the response latency to the thalamic spikes, M = 3.8 ± 1.5 ms (n = 9), with no significant difference across stimulation frequencies (p>0.05, one-way ANOVA), which suggests that the LGN is capable of monosynaptically driving V1 oscillatory activity at least up to 80 Hz without significant degradation of the entrainment.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of spike-triggered average data.

claim: There was no significant difference in response latency across stimulation frequencies.
source: We took the time of first negative peak of the STA as the response latency to the thalamic spikes, M = 3.8 ± 1.5 ms (n = 9), with no significant difference across stimulation frequencies (p>0.05, one-way ANOVA), which suggests that the LGN is capable of monosynaptically driving V1 oscillatory activity at least up to 80 Hz without significant degradation of the entrainment.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of response latency data.

claim: The LGN is capable of monosynaptically driving V1 oscillatory activity at least up to 80 Hz without significant degradation of the entrainment.
source: We took the time of first negative peak of the STA as the response latency to the thalamic spikes, M = 3.8 ± 1.5 ms (n = 9), with no significant difference across stimulation frequencies (p>0.05, one-way ANOVA), which suggests that the LGN is capable of monosynaptically driving V1 oscillatory activity at least up to 80 Hz without significant degradation of the entrainment.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed response latencies across stimulation frequencies.

claim: These functional coupling results support the notion that CaMKIIα thalamocortical projections can activate V1 circuits.
source: These functional coupling results thus support the notion that CaMKIIα thalamocortical projections can activate V1 circuits.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the functional coupling analysis.

claim: At 30 Hz frequency, only 3/16 sites were significantly modulated in spite of the high overall amplitude of the induced modulations.
source: At 30 Hz frequency, only 3/16 sites were significantly modulated in spite of the high overall amplitude of the induced modulations, likely because endogenously generated activations were already relatively prominent at this frequency.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of V1 LFP responses to different stimulation frequencies.

claim: With increasing frequency, a number of sites exhibited pronounced and significantly elevated spectral peaks at the stimulation frequency.
source: With increasing frequency, we found that a number of sites exhibited pronounced and significantly elevated spectral peaks at the stimulation frequency, consistent with direct thalamocortical drive reaching the V1 site (e.g. nine sites at 80 Hz stimulation, paired t-test: p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of V1 LFP responses to different stimulation frequencies.

claim: Higher frequency stimulation tended to result in enhanced hit rates and reduced false alarm rates.
source: We found higher frequency stimulation tended to result in enhanced hit rates and reduced false alarm rates.
evidence: The claim is supported by signal detection analysis of V1 LFP data.

claim: The sensitivity of V1 sites increased significantly with light stimulation frequency, reaching values of d' ≈ 2.0 at 80 Hz.
source: Converting these data to d' values, we found that indeed the sensitivity of V1 sites increased significantly with light stimulation frequency, reaching values of d' ≈ 2.0 at 80 Hz.
evidence: The claim is supported by signal detection analysis of V1 LFP data.

claim: For the frequencies used in the behavioral studies up to 50 Hz, the sensitivity of V1 LFPs appears to generally correspond to the sensitivity of the tree shrews at the behavioral level.
source: Note that for the frequencies used in the behavioral studies up to 50 Hz, the sensitivity of V1 LFPs appears to generally correspond to the sensitivity of the tree shrews at the behavioral level, that is, values in the range of 1–1.5.
evidence: The claim is a comparison between V1 LFP sensitivity and behavioral sensitivity.

claim: Robust transmembrane currents remain at 100 Hz light stimulation, but these are attenuated by a factor of around 70-fold relative to 10 Hz stimulation.
source: While robust transmembrane currents remain at 100 Hz light stimulation, these are attenuated by a factor of around 70-fold relative to 10 Hz stimulation compared to a 10-fold attenuation for 50 Hz light stimulation (Malyshev et al., 2015), and attenuation can be dependent on cell type and choice of AAV delivery system (Jackman et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Malyshev et al., 2015 and Jackman et al., 2014.

claim: The entrainment observed in this study indicates that CamKIIα-ChR2 expression in LGN neurons permits efficient activation of thalamocortical projections up to at least 80 Hz stimulation frequency.
source: The entrainment observed in this study nevertheless indicates that CamKIIα-ChR2 expression in LGN neurons permits efficient activation of thalamocortical projections up to at least 80 Hz stimulation frequency, and that V1 LFPs are sufficiently sensitive to permit accurate single-trial detection of LGN optogenetic stimulation.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the entrainment data.

claim: V1 LFPs are sufficiently sensitive to permit accurate single-trial detection of LGN optogenetic stimulation.
source: The entrainment observed in this study nevertheless indicates that CamKIIα-ChR2 expression in LGN neurons permits efficient activation of thalamocortical projections up to at least 80 Hz stimulation frequency, and that V1 LFPs are sufficiently sensitive to permit accurate single-trial detection of LGN optogenetic stimulation.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the V1 LFP sensitivity analysis.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the visual thalamic LGN triggers local neuronal circuit activity as well as an associated artificial visual percept that can be readily detected by the animals.
source: We demonstrate here that optogenetic activation of the visual thalamic LGN triggers local neuronal circuit activity as well as an associated artificial visual percept that can be readily detected by the animals.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: A previous report has provided proof of principle that electrical LGN stimulation can elicit artificial visual percepts in macaque monkey.
source: A previous report has already provided proof of principle that electrical LGN stimulation can elicit artificial visual percepts in macaque monkey (Pezaris and Reid, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pezaris and Reid, 2007.

claim: Tree shrews quickly generalized from the visual to the optogenetic task, suggestive of a visual nature of the evoked artificial percept.
source: As did the macaques in the previous study, tree shrews quickly generalized from the visual to the optogenetic task, suggestive of a visual nature of the evoked artificial percept.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed behavioral generalization.

claim: The overall task performance for optogenetic stimulation remained somewhat lower than the values observed during visual stimulation.
source: The overall task performance we observed for optogenetic stimulation remained somewhat lower than the values observed during visual stimulation, suggesting that artificially induced percepts were overall less readily detectable than visually induced percepts at the high contrast employed in this study.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of behavioral performance data.

claim: Artificially induced percepts were overall less readily detectable than visually induced percepts at the high contrast employed in this study.
source: The overall task performance we observed for optogenetic stimulation remained somewhat lower than the values observed during visual stimulation, suggesting that artificially induced percepts were overall less readily detectable than visually induced percepts at the high contrast employed in this study.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison of behavioral performance data.

claim: V1 responses scale with stimulus contrast.
source: Since V1 responses scale with stimulus contrast (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013), artificial stimulation detectability thus matches visual detectability at low to intermediate contrast values.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bhattacharyya et al., 2013.

claim: Artificial stimulation detectability matches visual detectability at low to intermediate contrast values.
source: Since V1 responses scale with stimulus contrast (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013), artificial stimulation detectability thus matches visual detectability at low to intermediate contrast values.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the relationship between V1 responses and stimulus contrast.

claim: Extensive training on detection of electrical microstimulation in V1 can be detrimental for detection of visual stimuli in macaques.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that for macaques, extensive training on detection of electrical microstimulation in V1 can be detrimental for detection of visual stimuli (Ni and Maunsell, 2010), consistent with an important role of behavioral strategy during optogenetic stimulus processing.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ni and Maunsell, 2010.

claim: The spatiotemporal configuration of light delivery and virus transfected neural elements including dendrites plays a crucial role in how optogenetic activation is translated into cortical activity and ultimately perception.
source: Indeed, computational modeling work relating to V1 suggests that the spatiotemporal configuration of light delivery and virus transfected neural elements including dendrites plays a crucial role in how optogenetic activation is translated into cortical activity and ultimately perception (Antolik et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Antolik et al., 2021.

claim: Optogenetic LGN stimulation, up to the light intensities tested here, produces robust artificial percepts that tree shrews can reliably detect in a suitable behavioral paradigm.
source: Our present results suggest that optogenetic LGN stimulation, up to the light intensities tested here, produces robust artificial percepts that tree shrews can reliably detect in a suitable behavioral paradigm.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Overly strong LGN stimulation has been shown to deactivate visual brain areas downstream of V1 for electrical stimulation.
source: Note that overly strong LGN stimulation is in any case undesirable as it has been shown to deactivate visual brain areas downstream of V1 for electrical stimulation (Logothetis et al., 2010), which would certainly compromise goal-directed behaviors based on artificial visual percepts.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Logothetis et al., 2010.

claim: Artificial stimulation necessarily co-activates both ON and OFF contrast channels, which never occurs in natural vision.
source: For example, since visually responsive ON- and OFF pathways are intermingled in LGN and layer 4 of V1 in most species including primates, artificial stimulation necessarily co-activates both contrast channels, which never occurs in natural vision since a part of the visual field can be bright or dark but not both at the same time (Beyeler et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Beyeler et al., 2017 and Nguyen et al., 2016.

claim: Such coactivation will produce cortical activation patterns not encountered during natural vision, potentially explaining the perceptual performance decrement for artificial vision.
source: Such coactivation will thus produce cortical activation patterns not encountered during natural vision, potentially explaining the perceptual performance decrement for artificial vision.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the impact of ON/OFF coactivation on perception.

claim: In the tree shrew LGN, ON- and OFF neurons tend to be segregated in separate layers.
source: In the tree shrew LGN, ON- and OFF neurons tend to be segregated in separate layers, with layers 1 and 2 containing ON cells, layers 4–5 containing OFF cells, layer 3 containing a mixed population, and layer 6 containing ON/OFF cells with an inhibitory surround Conway and Schiller, 1983; note that we have adopted the conventional labeling of the LGN layers as 1–6 from medial to lateral, whereas in Conway this ordering is reversed.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Conway and Schiller, 1983.

claim: Neural spiking activations linked to optogenetic stimulation were found particularly in LGN and for a small number of neurons also in V1.
source: We found neural spiking activations linked to optogenetic stimulation particularly in LGN and for a small number of neurons also in V1.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data analysis.

claim: Most neurons were activated by the onset of LGN optogenetic stimulation (ON-type response).
source: While most neurons were activated by the onset of LGN optogenetic stimulation (ON-type response), a minority of neurons interestingly exhibited significant OFF-type responses and were thus activated when the optogenetic stimulation ceased.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data analysis.

claim: A minority of neurons exhibited significant OFF-type responses and were activated when the optogenetic stimulation ceased.
source: While most neurons were activated by the onset of LGN optogenetic stimulation (ON-type response), a minority of neurons interestingly exhibited significant OFF-type responses and were thus activated when the optogenetic stimulation ceased.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data analysis.

claim: OFF-type responses are commonly observed to visual stimulation in the macaque.
source: OFF-type responses are commonly observed to visual stimulation, for example, in the macaque (Bair et al., 2002), where they tend to occur with shorter latencies than ON-type responses in both LGN and V1.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bair et al., 2002.

claim: In the macaque, OFF-type responses tend to occur with shorter latencies than ON-type responses in both LGN and V1.
source: OFF-type responses are commonly observed to visual stimulation, for example, in the macaque (Bair et al., 2002), where they tend to occur with shorter latencies than ON-type responses in both LGN and V1.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bair et al., 2002.

claim: In this study, OFF responses were delayed compared to ON responses with longer latencies of about 50 ms in both LGN and V1 for optogenetic stimulation.
source: In our study, we found the opposite effect for optogenetic stimulation in that the OFF responses were delayed compared to ON responses with longer latencies of about 50 ms in both LGN and V1.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data analysis.

claim: Due to the shorter latency and lower stimulus-linked variability, OFF responses might serve as a reference signal for temporal segregation of information by the visual system.
source: Bair and colleagues argue that due to the shorter latency and lower stimulus-linked variability, OFF responses might in fact serve as a reference signal for temporal segregation of information by the visual system.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the argument made by Bair and colleagues.

claim: Altered OFF responses following optogenetic stimulation might complicate perception and behavioral stimulus interpretation in artificial vision.
source: Altered OFF responses following optogenetic stimulation might thus complicate perception and behavioral stimulus interpretation in artificial vision.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the impact of altered OFF responses on perception.

claim: Laser-induced spikes in the LGN were reliably followed by depth negative potentials in V1 at a latency of ≈3 ms, which is similar to the latency of the V1 EPSP triggered by monosynaptic input from LGN neurons reported in the cat.
source: We found that laser-induced spikes in the LGN were reliably followed by depth negative potentials in V1 at a latency of ≈3 ms, which is similar to the latency of the V1 excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) triggered by monosynaptic input from LGN neurons reported in the cat (Sedigh-Sarvestani et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by spike-triggered average analysis and a citation to Sedigh-Sarvestani et al., 2017.

claim: The V1 LFP was spectrally coherent with evoked LGN spiking across the gamma frequency range (30–80 Hz).
source: Additionally, the V1 LFP was spectrally coherent with evoked LGN spiking across the gamma frequency range (30–80 Hz).
evidence: The claim is supported by spike field coherence analysis.

claim: Oscillatory activity in the gamma band has been associated with a number of visual processes.
source: As discussed above, oscillatory activity in the gamma band has been associated with a number of visual processes, and it is becoming increasingly clear that different frequencies of gamma activity are associated with different stimulus parameters.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Different frequencies of gamma activity are associated with different stimulus parameters.
source: As discussed above, oscillatory activity in the gamma band has been associated with a number of visual processes, and it is becoming increasingly clear that different frequencies of gamma activity are associated with different stimulus parameters.
evidence: The claim is stated as emerging knowledge in the field.

claim: The frequency of V1 gamma activity can be tuned through LGN optogenetic activation.
source: Here we were capable of tuning the frequency of V1 gamma activity through LGN optogenetic activation, a potentially important step in the development of visual prosthetics.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's findings on frequency-dependent V1 LFP responses.

claim: The relationship between LGN spiking and narrow band gamma activity in V1 has previously been shown to be coherent at both the level of V1 EPSC's, as well as the cortical LFP.
source: The relationship between LGN spiking and narrow band gamma activity in V1 has previously been shown to be coherent at both the level of V1 EPSC's, as well as the cortical LFP (Saleem et al., 2017; Schneider et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Saleem et al., 2017 and Schneider et al., 2021.

claim: This coherence is thought to be mitigated strictly by thalamocortical inputs.
source: Importantly this coherence is thought to be mitigated strictly by thalamocortical inputs, suggesting that a cortically driven neural prosthetic would be insufficient to generate thalamocortical coherence, which may be critical to the generation of organized visual percepts (Ribary, 2005).
